rule: Founder, 26 November 2026: an AI may research, organize sources and draft, and never approves its own historical claims. A published museum record is existing source material that itself needs review; it is not human-approved. A claim is approved by a named human reviewer with the right expertise, then by the museum's editor for wording, uncertainty and tone. The founder approves the product and its scope and is never recorded as the historical authority. Until reviewers are named, no new historical claim is published as verified and every entry stands as 'historical review pending'.

kinds.sourced: text or a fact taken from, or linked to, a museum record: existing source material, not yet reviewed by a person
kinds.uncertain: a claim the source gives as approximate or disputed, or one the game derives from a source
kinds.reconstruction: something shown as it might have looked, with no reviewed source behind it
kinds.fiction: invented for play, and said to be on the page
kinds.convention: a way of counting or naming, not a claim

entries.claim: The game is set in the emirate of Granada under the Nasrids and is called 'The Last Kingdom of al-Andalus'; the founder's design sets it in 1475.
entries.context: Title, subtitle and the opening brief
entries.uncertainty: The title is the founder's. The year 1475 is the design's and is not stated by a museum record as a year of anything; it is a setting, not an event.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The valley, its steward, its crops, prices and seasons are invented for play.
entries.context: The note on the opening brief ('This is a game, not a history')
entries.uncertainty: None: it is said to be invented.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Eleven real places are named, each where the museum places it, and the distances between them are measured from the museum's coordinates.
entries.context: The rules' regional distances; the records linked from the brief
entries.uncertainty: The coordinates are of the places today; the distances are straight lines over the globe, not roads of the time.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The brief links the museum's records of the Alhambra, the Generalife, the Nasrid palaces, the madrasa of Granada, the Nasrid entry into Granada, the building of the Alhambra, the fall of Granada, and Ibn al-Khatib's history of Granada.
entries.context: The opening brief, 'The setting, in the museum'
entries.uncertainty: The game states nothing about them itself: it shows each record's own label and links to it.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Five ideas behind the game's mechanics are linked to museum records: market inspection, matching soil and water, improvements to the water-lifting wheel, tiraz textiles, lustreware.
entries.context: The records the game links to for the ideas behind its mechanics
entries.uncertainty: The link says the idea is real, not that the game models it faithfully. The game's numbers are invented.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The look of the valley: lime-washed houses with clay-tile roofs and shuttered openings, one with an open gallery under its roof and one with a flat roof to walk on; a town wall with a tower and a round-arched gate; a mosque with a square minaret; a watermill with a wheel; a stone bridge of three arches; ox-carts; the dress of the people who walk.
entries.context: The 3D valley
entries.uncertainty: No museum record or reviewed source stands behind any of these shapes. They are the developer's general picture of a village of the western Mediterranean and are not stated anywhere as fact; under the founder's rule of 26 November 2026 they may not be presented as the architecture or dress of Nasrid Granada until a named reviewer has seen them.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent
entries.note: First for review when a reviewer is appointed. From 26 November 2026 the houses, wall, tower and gate are models authored ahead of time (gaming/art/blender/granada_town.py), surfaced with modern photographs of plaster, tile and stone that are of no particular place or time.

entries.claim: Wheat stands ripe in late spring, olives grow on a terrace behind a broken channel, a meadow waits for water; the scenario runs ninety-six days, to the end of winter.
entries.context: The fields and the calendar
entries.uncertainty: Invented for play and covered by the note on the brief.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The valley sends wheat, olives and olive oil by cart to "the port of Málaga", which pays its own prices and offers a contract for eight measures of oil; five measures of olives press to one of oil. Prices at the village and the port move by up to fifteen parts in a hundred with what each market holds. A load takes three days to reach the port by cart.
entries.context: The Economy panel: the port, the press, the contract
entries.uncertainty: Only the port's name is real. Its prices, its buyer, the contract, the carriage, the cart limit and the pressing ratio are numbers chosen for play; the panel says they are invented. Whether naming a real port beside invented trade misleads is for a reviewer to say. The way prices move is a rule made for play, not a description of any market. Three days is a number for play, set beside the straight-line distance the museum's coordinates give (89 km); no road, pace or journey time has been taken from a source.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The steward can place a house, a granary, a cistern that lets the pool hold more water, and a walled garden with a basin and cypresses, anywhere the ground allows.
entries.context: The Construction panel's catalogue and the four buildings as drawn
entries.uncertainty: Costs, sizes, days of work and effects are numbers chosen for play. The shapes are the game's own general picture of such buildings and copy none; whether a cistern and a walled garden of these forms suit a village of this time and place is for a reviewer to say.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: In the heat of summer a village downstream asks for part of the river's flow and offers to pay; sharing brings dinars and less water, refusing costs the households' goodwill because many have kin downstream.
entries.context: The decision "The village downstream asks for water", on the objectives panel
entries.uncertainty: The village, the request, the payment and every figure are invented, and the panel says so. How water was really shared between communities on one river, and by what custom or court, is a matter of history this decision does not describe and must not be read as describing; a reviewer should say whether the framing misleads.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Granada, Málaga, Almería and the Sierra Nevada stand where the map puts them; Málaga is 89 km from Granada and Almería 109 km, in straight lines; the coast runs through Málaga, Almuñécar and Almería.
entries.context: The region card on the Overview: a diagram of positions with a scale
entries.uncertainty: The coordinates are the museum's published records, which are source material and not reviewed fact. Distances are computed from them. The coast is three points joined by straight lines and is labelled as a sketch. The game's valley is marked west of the city and is invented; the route drawn to Málaga is a straight line, not a road.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: A second year, "The Merchants of Málaga": the port offers a contract for twelve measures of oil and one for a hundred and twenty of vegetables; the steward is asked to bring in 1,600 dinars by trade, keep a contract, house eighty households and build a cistern; the village downstream asks for water again.
entries.context: The second scenario: its brief, its tasks, its contracts, its decision
entries.uncertainty: Only the port's name is real. The contracts, the buyer, the goods traded, every price and every figure are invented for play, and the brief says so. Whether vegetables were carried to a port by cart, and what a valley of this kind sold, is for a reviewer.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: A third year, "A Dry Year": little snow lies on the mountain, the river runs at about three quarters of a usual year and less rain falls; the valley is asked to hold two cisterns and to keep its households faring well for sixty days.
entries.context: The third scenario: its brief, its river, its tasks, its decision
entries.uncertainty: The year, the river's three quarters, the link drawn between snow and the river, and every figure are invented for play, and the brief says so. Whether the river of such a valley follows the mountain's snow in this way, and how communities met a dry year, is for a reviewer.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The game calls itself 'a fictional city simulation inspired by records of Abbasid Baghdad and other historical institutions of the Islamic world'; costs, yields and prices are game numbers, not historical figures.
entries.context: Help, and the note beside the museum links
entries.uncertainty: The words are the founder's. 'Inspired by' is a claim of kinship, not of accuracy: the game is not, and does not say it is, a reconstruction. Whether the kinship is fair is a reviewer's question.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Each chapter's brief quotes the museum's own account of the history behind it and links two records.
entries.context: The briefs of the three chapters
entries.uncertainty: The words quoted are the museum's summaries, unaltered; the game adds none of its own.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Each tool and building is linked to the museum's record of the real thing behind it.
entries.context: The construction tools and their descriptions
entries.uncertainty: The link says the thing is real, not that the building in the game works as it did.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Each research project is linked to a museum record.
entries.context: The research panel
entries.uncertainty: As above.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: An endowment sets a sum aside for ever, and its yield pays a public building's upkeep: 'the game's form of the waqf'.
entries.context: Chapter 3, the Endow tool
entries.uncertainty: The principle (the principal kept, the yield given) is the museum's record; the sums and the rule that a building then costs nothing are the game's.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Droughts, silted canals and fevers that 'come with the caravans' strike the district.
entries.context: The events of each chapter
entries.uncertainty: Invented events in a fictional district. Under the founder's rule they are to be shown with mitigation and recovery, not as spectacle: a hospital, a granary and a cleared canal are the game's answers.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The look of the district: houses, domes, a bath, a library, a hospital, a water wheel.
entries.context: The 3D district
entries.uncertainty: No museum record or reviewed source stands behind these shapes. They are generic and are not stated as the architecture of Abbasid Baghdad; they may not be presented as such until reviewed.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Every round takes its name, its place, its coordinates and its year from one museum record: 2,125 rounds at 568 places in the pack.
entries.context: Every round of every day
sources: the museum records named in gaming/games/atlas/data/pack.v1.json, by id
entries.uncertainty: The game writes no statement of history of its own. Each record carries its own sources and its own uncertainty; a year or a place that is approximate in the record is approximate in the game, and the score allows for the record's precision.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The region shown by the hint is the museum's own name for the region the place lies in.
entries.context: The region hint
sources: the museum's region names, as read by gaming/games/atlas/tools/build-pack.ts
entries.uncertainty: Regions are broad and modern in their naming; a region without a name in all seven languages is not offered.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Centuries are counted as historians count them: 701 to 800 is the eighth.
entries.context: The century estimate
entries.uncertainty: A convention, not a claim.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: 263 events named for one place and scored at another are held out of the game.
entries.context: The pack; gaming/games/atlas/data/review.v1.json
entries.uncertainty: These are questions for the museum's data, not statements by the game: each is listed with the record to look at.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The Atlas of Stories, the storm that scattered it, the ink moths, Hudhud, the Storykeeper, the workshop, its cat, its mirrors on stands and every line spoken in the scene are invented for play.
entries.context: The note under the picture and the museum note at the end ('This is a game, not a history')
entries.uncertainty: None: it is said to be invented. Since 26 November 2026 every line the scholar speaks also carries the words 'Imagined words, not a quotation' beside his name, in seven languages.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Ibn al-Haytham let light into a dark room through a small hole to test that it travels in straight lines and that a solid body cuts it; the scene's beam goes straight until a mirror turns it or the tower of books stops it.
entries.context: The puzzle's rule; the scholar's lines d_scholar_2 and d_scholar_dark_1; museum note note_2
entries.uncertainty: The record describes tests with sunlight, moonlight and lamps and a ruler; the mirrors at fixed angles on a grid are the game's own device, and the line about stopping the beam with a hand paraphrases 'cut with an opaque body'.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Until 26 November 2026 a glass prism spread the beam into colours on the Atlas page. It has been taken out of the scene.
entries.context: Formerly the prism above the reading stand and the rainbow beam; now only the museum note, which says why no prism is shown
entries.uncertainty: No museum record read for this scene says Ibn al-Haytham worked with a glass prism. It was in the scene because both of the founder's pictures for this subject show one. An independent review named it as unsupported and the founder's directive of 26 November 2026 (section 11) has it removed unless a reviewer approves a historically honest use; none has. The rule for a prism remains in the game's code, unused.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent
entries.note: Removed by the agent on the founder's directive; this is not a reviewer's decision, and the entry stays pending for one.

entries.claim: He held that light goes from the thing to the eye, against older books that had sight go out from the eye.
entries.context: The optional line d_scholar_see_1, spoken since 26 November 2026 by the Atlas's own voice as what the museum's record says, not by the scholar as his own sentence; museum note note_3
entries.uncertainty: The museum's prose attributes this to the Encyclopaedia of Islam and names Euclid, Ptolemy and al-Kindi on the other side; the game's line says only 'some old books'.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Ibn al-Haytham was born in Basra around 965 and later lived in Cairo; his best-known book is on optics.
entries.context: Museum note note_1
entries.uncertainty: The record gives the birth as 'around 354 AH/965' and notes that the reports of his death differ; the note gives no year of death.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: With the curtain drawn, the town outside appears on the workshop wall, upside down.
entries.context: The secret behind the curtain cord; lines d_secret_1 to d_secret_3
entries.uncertainty: The record read for this scene describes lights passing through one hole and falling on the wall each opposite its own source, and the museum's prose says a treatise of his sets out the dark room for watching eclipses. That a whole view appears turned over follows from the first; neither record says he described a picture of a town. Since 26 November 2026 the picture falls on the drawn curtain, which is the side opposite the hole; before that it was drawn on the back wall, which an independent review named as wrong.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The scholar's face, turban and robe, the room, the garden and the roofs through the arch.
entries.context: Everything drawn in the scene
entries.uncertainty: No portrait of Ibn al-Haytham from his own time is known to the museum; the figure follows the founder's pictures, which are themselves imaginings. The house and the skyline are composites that stand for no real building or city; clothing and architecture have not been checked for place and century.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Fifty subjects are grouped in ten worlds of five.
entries.context: The game's structure; gaming/games/hudhud/src/content/atlas.v1.json
entries.uncertainty: The grouping is a structure for play, taken from the founder's instruction; it does not say that the five of a world lived together. Each subject's own claims will be entered here when its quest is written. Three joins need a reviewer's eye first: the Sailor of Sohar (no person is named and only the port has a record), Sindbad (joined to the Thousand and One Nights, not to the museum's Book of Sindbad, which is another work) and the two thumbnail titles for al-Khwarizmi.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The player's explorer is a girl or a boy with a choice of skin, clothes and hair or headwear. The clothes are one generic tunic and vest and are the dress of no named region or century.
entries.context: The first screen and Settings; docs/gaming/hudhud/explorers.md
entries.uncertainty: Nothing on the page says where or when the clothes are from. The founder has asked for explorers from different regions over a thousand years; a roster of twelve is proposed and none is drawn, because dress by place and century must be reviewed first.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: In al-Jazari's elephant clock, every half hour figures move, a ball passes from the falcon to the dragon to a vessel with a gong and comes to rest in a bowl, and the balls gathered tell the time elapsed. One reference work dates his book of machines to 1205.
entries.context: The elephant clock quest: the order of the five parts on the ball's road, the answer to 'Ask about the balls', the museum note (gaming/games/hudhud/src/content/clock.ts; strings ck_balls_1, ck_note_2)
entries.uncertainty: Taken from the museum's record, which cites the Metropolitan Museum's catalogue entry and TDV; the record itself has not been through historical review. The quest shows the parts as a row on a workbench, which no source describes.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Inside the elephant is a float with a small hole that fills and sinks in a set time; the hole was widened little by little until that time was half an hour. The bird's whistle is air pushed out by the sinking float, and a ball's weight moves the rider's arms.
entries.context: The elephant clock quest: the answer to 'Ask about the float' (ck_float_1); the bird answering to the sinking float and the rider to a ball (content/clock.ts)
entries.uncertainty: From the museum's prose on the record, after Hill's 1974 translation of al-Jazari. The game says 'half an hour' where the prose says the hole is enlarged until filling and sinking take the required time, and names half-hour timing in the next sentence: a reviewer should confirm the wording. The record warns that this establishes no rate for any copy or replica.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: Each part of the clock 'answers to' one motion and 'hands on' another in a single row: the float's sinking makes the falcon let its ball go. The workbench, the muddle of parts, the apprentice and every spoken line are the game's own.
entries.context: The elephant clock quest as a whole; the museum note says so (ck_note_1, ck_note_3)
entries.uncertainty: A simplification for play. What was read for the game does not say how the falcon is made to release its ball; the record describes levers, chains, strings and pulleys inside the elephant. The apprentice is an invented, unnamed girl. Al-Jazari's one line is marked on the page as imagined words.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The opening story's frame is invented for play: a quiet museum, a great book called the Atlas of Stories, a storm that blows a window open and scatters fifty pages over ten worlds, and a hoopoe named Hudhud who lives among the museum's shelves. The fifth panel says so: 'The Atlas and the storm are invented.'
entries.context: The five panels of the opening story shown before the Atlas (pro_1 to pro_5), and the museum note on the Atlas (hub_note)
entries.uncertainty: None: it is said to be invented. The fifth panel also says the people and places behind the pages are real, or stories marked as stories; each page's own claims are entered separately.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-fable-5-2), an AI agent

entries.claim: The museum's record says al-Kindi wrote the earliest treatise on breaking ciphers that survives. In it he counts the letters of a long sample of the language, ranks them from most to fewest, and compares that with the symbols of the secret message.
entries.context: The al-Kindi quest: the answer to 'Ask how to begin' and the first part of the museum note (gaming/games/hudhud/src/content/cipher.ts; strings cf_count_1, cf_note_2)
entries.uncertainty: Taken from the museum's record of the method, which cites the 1987 Damascus edition of his treatise and TDV; the record itself has not been through historical review. A reviewer should check that 'earliest that survives' is the record's wording after TDV (the earliest surviving treatise, with earlier concealment acknowledged) and not 'first ever', and that 'a long sample of the language' matches the record's 'a sample of a known language'.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent

entries.claim: He warns that a short message can mislead. And he tests a guess by looking at which letters stand side by side and at the usual openings of messages.
entries.context: The al-Kindi quest: the answer to 'Ask about short messages' and the second part of the museum note (strings cf_short_1, cf_note_2); the Challenge puzzle's short message that ranking alone gets wrong (content/cipher.ts)
entries.uncertainty: From the museum's prose on the record, after the 1987 edition. A reviewer should check the exact sense of the short-sample warning (the record says a short message may depart from ordinary usage and a guess needs checking against letter combinations and context) and that 'the usual openings of messages' is how the record puts conventional openings. The Challenge puzzle is the game's own illustration of the warning, not a case from his treatise.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent

entries.claim: The game uses drawn signs in place of Arabic letters, a page of the Atlas that the storm turned into secret marks, a fixed opening of two signs on every page (the feather, then the sun), the young messenger, and one imagined line for al-Kindi ('Do not guess. Count first, then compare.'). The three ways of playing and their rows are the game's own.
entries.context: The al-Kindi quest as a whole; the museum note says so (cf_note_1, cf_note_3, cf_note_4)
entries.uncertainty: A simplification for play. Al-Kindi worked with the letters of Arabic; the signs are the game's, so that the puzzle is the same in every language. The two-sign opening is a game rule standing in for the record's 'usual openings of messages'; the record does not say pages of any book began with a fixed opening. The messenger is an invented child. Al-Kindi's one line is marked on the page as imagined words. The note also says that the record calls the treatise the earliest that survives and does not say he invented all secret writing: a reviewer should check that this line keeps the record's limit.
entries.author: Claude Code (claude-sonnet-5-5), an AI agent
